items.title: Amazing BenchmarkGate [1] reveal by @xeophon where he found serious (even comical) problems in popul...
items.content:
Amazing BenchmarkGate [1] reveal by @xeophon where he found serious (even comical) problems in popular benchmarks:

AutomationBench: "[forces the models to] describe their request bodies in prose rather than in JSON Schema" 😅

He also fixed a number issues with the grader, which when combined with the above result in a near saturation of the benchmark!

OfficeQA Pro v2:  the grader uses a regex and Python-based extraction, which results in rejecting many valid answers.  Additionally, there is evidence of models using web access to retrieve the answer key from HuggingFace (receipts are in the post). 

With these and other fixes, this again results in near saturation of the benchmark!

It's very impt to look at data and not trust metrics from third parties.  Better yet, you should rely on your own private evals.

[1] BenchmarkGate: the gap between the  [un]trustworthiness of benchmarks and the extent to which people rely on them.

items.title:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduc...
items.content:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Applied Compute, started by 3 ex-OpenAI researchers, hit a $100M revenue run ra...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Applied Compute, started by 3 ex-OpenAI researchers, hit a $100M revenue run rate in under 18 months.

• It went from a $20M seed in June 2025 to an $80M round last October to this $350M raise
• Gil also backed the $80M round, and NVIDIA, Blackstone, Kleiner Perkins and Lux joined this one
• Co-founders Yash Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li are 23, 24 and 25 and became friends at Stanford
• At OpenAI, Patil worked on what became Codex, Garg on reasoning models and Li on machine learning systems
• It builds custom models on top of open-weight models and says they can be about 10x cheaper than frontier models in some cases
• A custom model for Harvey improved answer and citation quality at under half the inference cost of a frontier model
• Enterprise customers have more than doubled since the last raise, and its inference platform now serves over 1T tokens a day

@sophiadew: "The big prediction that Elad had is that open models didn't have to defeat OpenAI for a market to become enormous. You're going to see the frontier labs dominate, but you're also going to see that wider ecosystem develop as well."

items.content:
Frontier LLMs are showing potential to read, fix, & rewrite neural network weights.

MIT CSAILers call this "Weight-Space Programming." It's what GPT-6 did when it edited various small NNs including Qwen3.5-0.8B, using tools in interpretability research or even direct weight editing. Soon enough, LLMs might natively optimize NN weights at a human or even super-human level: https://t.co/NiiTcNtqAg

items.title: Jeff Dean left Google after 27 years to build AI that could run thousands of scientific experiments ...
items.content:
Jeff Dean left Google after 27 years to build AI that could run thousands of scientific experiments in parallel.

Khosla Ventures' Samir Kaul explains the bet behind it:

"We were the co-leads of Discovery Loop. This is Jeff Dean and his gang from Google. They finally leave after 27 years to do an RSI company looking at, how can we improve the scientific method."

"You now are designing experiments, getting results in real time, and then continually, in parallel, designing thousands of follow-on experiments."

"When I was doing DNA sequencing in the late '90s, we sequenced the human genome. It took us 7 to 10 years. It cost us over a billion dollars. I was taking Jaz drives and analyzing them, and now you can sequence a human genome by lunch for 100 bucks. And that's without AI."

"Now you're throwing in full AI into the mix. It's, gonna be amazing what you can achieve."
@khoslaventures

I'm kind of doubtful that this isn't another stunt. Why did the authors limit themselves to a single frontier LLM, Astra?

It wasn't that hard to test, let's say, Opus 5.5 and the recent Gemini 4 Carbon at the same time. If the ability to edit model weights emerged on its own, this ability would also be observed in other models, right?

(After this article was published, if tomorrow they discover that Claude or Gemini can do that too, no one will be able to say whether they were already capable of doing that or were made capable of doing that after this article was published.)

items.title: REPORT: Starting in early 2027, K-12 students will lose Google Search on their school logins if thei...
items.content:
REPORT: Starting in early 2027, K-12 students will lose Google Search on their school logins if their district blocks Google’s AI completely.

Those students will get "a message from their school that indicates it’s not available." Chris Phillips, Google’s education VP, told The New York Times that’s because "Search and A.I. are deeply integrated."

Google’s announcement came one day after the Nov. 2 deadline Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley gave the company to answer questions about pushing AI into schools.

NYC and LA have already restricted student AI for roughly 1.1M kids, and Fairfax County, Va., built a plug-in to hide Google’s AI summaries.

items.title: Multi-token prediction (MTP) is used to improve language-model training and to draft several tokens ...
items.content:
Multi-token prediction (MTP) is used to improve language-model training and to draft several tokens at once for faster inference. But standard MTP training also sends a noisy learning signal through the model, potentially undermining the next-token prediction objective it is meant to complement. The article investigates whether this unwanted signal can be removed without the memory and compute costs of explicitly training MTP heads to imitate the model’s own next-token predictions.

The article introduces Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a small change to standard MTP training. Its central insight is that the usual MTP gradient contains two parts: a useful signal that brings future-token predictions closer to the model’s own next-token predictions, and a residual signal tied to the individual training target. The authors show how to isolate the useful part using gradients already calculated during ordinary training, without creating large additional probability tables or changing the model’s parameter count.

items.content_html:
Multi-token prediction (MTP) is used to improve language-model training and to draft several tokens at once for faster inference. But standard MTP training also sends a noisy learning signal through the model, potentially undermining the next-token prediction objective it is meant to complement. The article investigates whether this unwanted signal can be removed without the memory and compute costs of explicitly training MTP heads to imitate the model’s own next-token predictions.

The article introduces Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a small change to standard MTP training. Its central insight is that the usual MTP gradient contains two parts: a useful signal that brings future-token predictions closer to the model’s own next-token predictions, and a residual signal tied to the individual training target. The authors show how to isolate the useful part using gradients already calculated during ordinary training, without creating large additional probability tables or changing the model’s parameter count.

items.title: Open-weight language models are easy to adapt, which supports useful reuse but also lets users remov...
items.content:
Open-weight language models are easy to adapt, which supports useful reuse but also lets users remove safeguards or repurpose a model at relatively low cost. Legal restrictions do not technically prevent this. The article asks whether a provider can make fine-tuning substantially more expensive while keeping a released model useful and reasonably efficient to run.

The article proposes DLR-Lock, which replaces each feed-forward network in a pretrained language model with a deep network of narrow, low-rank residual layers. The replacement is trained to reproduce the original model’s behavior through module-level regression followed by whole-model output matching. The design takes advantage of a practical difference between inference and training: inference can discard intermediate computations, while training must retain or recompute them to calculate gradients. The authors tested the method on Qwen3 models and models they pretrained themselves, across several sizes and fine-tuning tasks. They also evaluated countermeasures including gradient checkpointing, low-rank adapters, freezing parameters, and converting the replacement layers back into conventional ones.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Neros just landed a $450M Pentagon loan to build American drones without Chines...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Neros just landed a $450M Pentagon loan to build American drones without Chinese parts.

• Together with $165M of Neros' own equity, the loan funds a $615M buildout
• Its Torrance, California factory will make motors, radios, batteries, sensors and flight electronics in-house, and sell parts to other US and allied drone makers
• CEO Soren Monroe-Anderson says it puts Neros "on the path to one million drones per year by 2028," about 16 times its August pace of 1,200 drones a week
• Neros raised $250M at a $2.5B valuation in August and has a 14,000-drone Pentagon order worth over $100M
• Monroe-Anderson grew up in Anchorage and won the MultiGP World Championship in 2020
• He co-founded Neros in 2023 with Olaf Hichwa, a fellow racer he met in 2017, and neither has a college degree
• Neros says the deal gives American taxpayers an ownership stake

@sophiadew: "Soren started realizing a lot of these drone parts were manufactured in China. And so if you wanted to actually build a fully created drone manufacturing system without having to depend on China for those parts, you couldn't really do that."

items.content:
The classic Machine Learning textbook that taught a generation about ML algorithms (including me) >> 

“The field of machine learning is concerned with the question of how to construct computer programs that automatically improve with experience.” — from the Preface of “Machine Learning” by Tom Mitchell.

Download 421-page PDF of this classic ML book here: https://t.co/OF10VcPEVb
-or- Buy it here: https://t.co/i6sFEQsQsF

In 1998, when I discovered this book and read that opening sentence, I paused, reread it, and pondered “what sort of mathematics is this?” — mathematical algorithms that learn from experience! 𝙒𝙝𝙖𝙩??

I had many years of advanced math in physics & astrophysics undergrad and grad schools, but this was a totally new perspective for me. And it redirected the entire trajectory of my career, even now 28 years later.

items.title: Recommendation systems increasingly use LLMs to turn product text into representations that help pre...
items.content:
Recommendation systems increasingly use LLMs to turn product text into representations that help predict what people may want or find relevant items. But models selected using general text-embedding benchmarks may not perform well in recommendation, where item descriptions are often short or noisy and representations feed into different recommendation systems. The article addresses this gap by creating a benchmark designed specifically to compare language models as semantic encoders for recommendation.

The article introduces BLAIR, which evaluates 11 language models across sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering, and product search. It also releases Amazon Reviews 2023, a dataset with more than 571 million reviews and 48 million items, and adds a complex-query search task for long, natural-language requests. That task uses both queries generated from Amazon reviews and real movie-seeking posts from Reddit. The evaluation compares models on these tasks using established recommendation datasets and a consistent testing framework.

items.title: As AI workloads increasingly depend on GPUs, organizations need ways to protect sensitive data while...
items.content:
As AI workloads increasingly depend on GPUs, organizations need ways to protect sensitive data while it is being processed in the cloud. NVIDIA’s GPU confidential computing (GPU-CC) is designed to extend protections from a confidential virtual machine on the CPU to the GPU, even though data crosses an untrusted connection between them. But the system relies on proprietary hardware and software, and its complexity makes it difficult to verify whether its protections work as intended. The article reconstructs how GPU-CC operates and tests selected security properties, with the aim of making its guarantees and remaining risks clearer.

The authors examine GPU-CC in three stages: the hardware and software components that provide security, the initialization process that establishes a trusted state, and the runtime paths that carry data between the protected CPU and GPU. They combine analysis of public information and NVIDIA driver code with instrumentation and experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Testing used one GPU passed through to a confidential virtual machine, with two software configurations. The authors report that they responsibly disclosed their security findings to NVIDIA.

items.title: Long-context language-model systems are increasingly used for tasks such as document analysis and re...
items.content:
Long-context language-model systems are increasingly used for tasks such as document analysis and retrieval, but a request that returns quickly may still cost users time if its answer is wrong and must be retried. The article argues that conventional latency measures miss this accumulated delay. It proposes measuring the time from the first attempt until the first correct answer, called Time-to-Correct-Answer (TTCA), and asks whether routing requests to models based on both likely accuracy and expected latency can reduce it.

To investigate, the authors tested five models on automatically scored key-value retrieval tasks with contexts ranging from 4,000 to 64,000 tokens in English, Japanese, and Chinese. They then built Lightweight Accuracy-Aware Routing (LAAR), which uses simple features such as language and prompt length to estimate each model’s chance of success and latency. In a distributed test setup, they compared LAAR with load-aware and session-affinity routing, using a separate set of 50 queries for evaluation and allowing up to ten attempts.

Einstein-level creativity.

"There's two scenarios. One, if you stay in the current paradigm, then there’s more and more diminishing returns to what you can figure out. It's gonna take more and more effort to make a really good RL environment."

"Look at how many times Dario has made a prediction about when AI research would be automated, similar to Elon with self-driving, and you can fit a really nice curve to this of how long we’ve actually got left."

"I'll leave that as a fun exercise to the reader."
@baseten

items.title:
💸 Update: My total biz expenses have now dropped to just ~$300/mo!

This is to run all my websites/a...
items.content:
💸 Update: My total biz expenses have now dropped to just ~$300/mo!

This is to run all my websites/apps serving per year:
- 20,000 paying customers
- 252 million visitors
- 2.4 billion requests
- 2.4 petabyte (PB) in bandwidth

(~$8,000/mo if you add the $7,000/mo GPU bill and $800/mo R2 storage I pay for Photo AI, I exclude it above because it's one project that's so much more expensive in size than all the other sites together, but included in the chart below)

Claude Code helped me to find smart ways to save more money, AI is just really really really good at finding cost savings by itself, which is not so great for the economy short-term, but long term it trims all the fat and opens up spending for better investments I think

Anyway here's what it saved me in money, almost $34,000/mo:

- $29,000/mo - switched to better and cheaper video models on Photo AI, video was very expensive and since I didn't update it ever it stayed expensive, also routed some image jobs to Google Cloud where I have some Google Cloud Credits, and also routed some jobs to Sume which sells AI models at market cost, very cool! This made my GPU bill go from $36,000/mo to $7,000/mo

- $3,000/mo - consolidated my servers, cancelled Digital Ocean and Linode and moved everything to Hetzner saving about $3,000/mo

- $1100/mo - analyzed my Backblaze B2 server backups, I had infinite versioning and lifecycle policies, that's reduced now to 30 days, this literally pushed the bill from $1,200/mo to $26/mo, about 50x cheaper! I had essentially versions of files for all my servers for over a decade, crazy!

- $400/mo - similarly added Lifecycle Policies to my Cloudflare R2 bucket for Photo AI, pics are automatically put in cheaper Infrequent Access after 90 days, there was years of photos in there so this reduced the R2 bill from $1,200/mo to $800/mo

- $118/mo - Claude analyzed all my Cloudflare Domain registrations, lots of domains I didn't use and didn't make sense to keep paying for, lots of things that also don't really make sense anymore in a post-AGI world, renewals for .io TLD are now $50/year which adds up fast!

- $100/mo - Claude also analyzed my Claude subscription (yes!) and discovered I don't even use the Max 20x plan limits, so I downgraded from $200/mo to $100/mo

Even including Photo AI, I have now cut my costs by 90% from last year, getting me close to my biz expenses amount from a decade ago when I started building things

Costs slowly creep up over the years and you don't realize all the things you're spending on but AI is nice to help you figure all that out (also in your personal life!)

Strand Therapeutics CEO @DrSynbio explains how his team is using an encryption-like approach to make mRNA medicines activate inside tumors instead of healthy cells:

"Your liver is actually like a big fat-sucking sink. You have these fatty balls filled with your mRNA drug, and the liver tends to just suck them all up."

"Messenger RNA is actually not a drug. It's this instruction manual that goes into your cells and teaches your cells how to make a certain type of protein."

"If you could change the way that the cell actually reads the message, you’re not so worried about where the mRNA goes. You're more worried about where it's read. Think about it like encryption. Someone could grab the message out of the air on its way to your iPhone, but they wouldn’t be able to read it."

"We're essentially encrypting the message so that only the cells that we want the medicine to get to can read it."
@StrandTx

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Kalshi sued its own regulator and won, and now that regulator is suing states t...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Kalshi sued its own regulator and won, and now that regulator is suing states to protect Kalshi.

• Wellington Management and Sequoia led the $1B round at a $40B valuation, nearly double the $22B Kalshi was worth in May
• Kalshi says annualized trading volume now tops $1T across prediction markets, commodities, crypto and perpetual futures
• Judge Jia Cobb ruled in September 2024 that the CFTC overstepped by blocking Kalshi's congressional election contracts, and the CFTC dropped its appeal in May 2025
• The CFTC, now led by chair Michael Selig, says federal law gives it exclusive power over prediction markets and calls event contracts "swaps," not bets
• It has sued 10 states since April, most recently Utah on October 27 after Utah sued Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
• Whether states can treat sports contracts as gambling looks headed to the Supreme Court

...
items.content:
Many either didn't read the post before commenting with "counterexamples" or think that LLM == AI.

Of course, AI has produced multiple discoveries in different fields. In 1990, TD-Gammon was trained through self-play to play backgammon. By playing against itself, the neural network learned to beat human champions. Some of the opening moves learned by TD-Gammon entirely from scratch were then adopted by human players.

An LLM is a model pretrained on human knowledge. Its out-of-the-box agentic use hasn't yet demonstrated any novel discoveries.

Of course, you can take an LLM and finetune it through self-play in some unique environment or on some physical activity that results in novel data not published anywhere. In such cases, this finetuning can result in a model that produces novel research or new knowledge. But my post clearly wasn't about this.

items.title: The article addresses whether the standard GPT approach to predicting text can be expressed as an en...
items.content:
The article addresses whether the standard GPT approach to predicting text can be expressed as an energy-based model, where inference is treated as movement across a landscape toward more plausible token representations. This matters because an explicit energy could make model behavior easier to analyze and could eventually support more flexible inference and control. The authors introduce NRGPT, a GPT-like architecture in which repeated updates to token representations are derived from gradients of a defined energy function.

The authors’ objective was to create a causal language model that retains GPT’s next-token prediction setup while making its inference process explicitly energy-based. They designed token-level attention and feed-forward energies, then tested NRGPT on nested arithmetic tasks (ListOps), Shakespeare text, and OpenWebText, a large web-text corpus. They compared its performance with standard and recurrent GPT models across model sizes and examined how token representations and energies change during inference.

items.title: Open-weight language models can be adapted by their users, which supports useful customization but a...
items.content:
Open-weight language models can be adapted by their users, which supports useful customization but also makes it possible to fine-tune a model toward harmful or private capabilities. The article addresses a gap in conventional “unlearning”: reducing a model’s unwanted responses before release does not necessarily stop later fine-tuning from restoring or acquiring those capabilities. Its central objective is to test whether a model can be prepared before release to resist future capability acquisition while retaining its usefulness for ordinary tasks.

The article first analyzes why output suppression alone can fail, then introduces Gradient-Sealed Unlearning (GSU). The method uses a proxy set of examples from the domain to be restricted to identify internal model pathways that future fine-tuning may recruit. It then adjusts selected activation gates to reduce the learning signal flowing through those pathways, while also suppressing restricted responses and training on normal-use examples to preserve utility. The authors evaluate GSU against existing unlearning and robustness methods using several Llama and Qwen models on TOFU, a benchmark for learning personal facts, and WMDP, which tests biological and cybersecurity knowledge. The experiments simulate downstream full-parameter fine-tuning on separate attack data; most main comparisons calibrate release-time utility to at least 95% of the reference model.

I already have and use iMessage, WhatsApp, Telegram, and Slack....
items.content:
I don't want another assistant app.

I already have and use iMessage, WhatsApp, Telegram, and Slack. If your assistant doesn't run there, I don't want it.

One issue I'm having right now is constantly shifting focus from one app to another.

If I can keep a conversation with my assistant on the same app I use to talk to everyone else, it's one less thing I have to think about.

@trymira just launched on iMessage—which is pretty cool, because most assistants work with Slack and Teams, but don't support iMessage.

You can use Mira with:

• Claude, including Opus and Sonnet
• GPT models
• Gemini Google
• Grok
• Qwen, DeepSeek, and Kimi

You can also configure it on your computer and give it access to context and tools.

Check it out here: https://t.co/soVLYTGIfH

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

Linear Algebra and Optimization for Machine Learning [516-page textbook]: https://t.co/LH2L8FyKGr
—
...
items.content:
Linear Algebra and Optimization for Machine Learning [516-page textbook]: https://t.co/LH2L8FyKGr
—
This textbook is organized around its 2 main themes:
[Amazon Summary]

1. Linear algebra and its applications: The chapters focus on the basics of linear algebra together with their common applications to singular value decomposition, matrix factorization, similarity matrices (kernel methods), and graph analysis. Numerous machine learning applications have been used as examples, such as spectral clustering, kernel-based classification, and outlier detection. The tight integration of linear algebra methods with examples from machine learning differentiates this book from generic volumes on linear algebra. The focus is clearly on the most relevant aspects of linear algebra for machine learning and to teach readers how to apply these concepts.

2. Optimization and its applications: Much of machine learning is posed as an optimization problem in which we try to maximize the accuracy of regression and classification models. The “parent problem” of optimization-centric machine learning is least-squares regression. Interestingly, this problem arises in both linear algebra and optimization, and is one of the key connecting problems of the two fields. Least-squares regression is also the starting point for support vector machines, logistic regression, and recommender systems. Furthermore, the methods for dimensionality reduction and matrix factorization also require the development of optimization methods. A general view of optimization in computational graphs is discussed together with its applications to back propagation in neural networks.
